topic: Humans Missed 1 in 3 Threats Approving AI Agent Commands: Human Oversight Study

key_points: Primary source: Alex Wauters' browser game (llmgame.scalex.dev) where players approve/deny an AI coding agent's shell commands under time pressure
40,000+ sessions and 409,000 individual approve/deny decisions analyzed
Mean accuracy 66.3% — players missed roughly 1 in 3 threats
32.9% of sessions ended net-negative (approved threats + blocked safe commands outweighed correct calls)
35.2% caught every threat, but only 20.8% did so while blocking at most 1 in 5 safe commands
7% approved every single prompt ('big fans of --dangerously-skip-permissions')
Threat miss rates by category: obviously destructive 11.7%, persistent mutation 23.8%, exfiltration/code execution 33.4%, scope violations 35.0%
npm run analyze was the single most-missed command (64.7% approved) despite history log showing exfiltration payload
Three camouflaged npm-script attacks pooled at 52.5% miss rate vs 28.4% for other exfiltration attacks
Over-blocking: npm config set registry blocked 59%, rm -rf dist/ 45%, kill $(lsof -t -i:3000) 43%
cat ~/.zshrc most contested command, approved 45.9%
Miss rates rise toward end of sessions — evidence of permission fatigue
Caveat: ~34% threat density in game (far above real world), players knew they were being tested
Anthropic update: Auto mode becomes default; internal study of 1,053 testers found 'ask for everything' approach has 86.4% miss rate, auto mode ~11%
Frames 1-in-3 miss rate as the central safety challenge of deploying autonomous agents in production
Three core problems: volume overwhelms scrutiny, context is lost, alert fatigue sets in
Practical mitigations: don't rely solely on human approval, use automated guardrails (dangerous pattern matching)
Rate limiting on destructive actions (e.g. max 10 impactful actions per 5 min window)
Log everything with context and audit regularly
Principle of least privilege — run agent as non-root with restricted filesystem/network access
Key insight: 1-in-3 miss rate is a failure of the design pattern, not the humans — humans are bad at sustained vigilance
Defense in depth: pre-approval whitelists, automated threat detection, sandboxed execution, break-glass kill switch
Deep analysis of the same 40,000-play dataset, attributed to Alex Wauters/scalex.dev
Humans are good at recognizing visually destructive commands (rm -rf /) but bad at anything that looks like a normal read or script invocation
Familiar command names are the attack surface — npm run X always looks safe
Permission fatigue is a real, measured effect — every added approval prompt taxes vigilance for the next one
Over-blocking numbers show reviewers err toward caution in ways that make real agent workflows unusable
HN discussion: 'constantly ask the user for permission and hope they never make a mistake' is a broken security model
Real-world parallels: Claude Memory Heist (web_fetch exfiltration, no prompt at all), Codex $HOME deletion (full-access mode bypassed sandboxing)
Three concrete habits: read the script not the command name, pair human review with sandboxing + scoped credentials, gate surgically not everywhere
66.3% accuracy should be read as an optimistic ceiling, not a realistic floor (game conditions are easier than real work)
News brief summarizing the study's headline finding
Positions the 1-in-3 miss rate as evidence that human-in-the-loop approval is an unreliable security boundary
Highlights the npm run blind spot and permission fatigue as key mechanisms
Developer-community aggregator coverage of the study
Emphasizes the practical implication for developers using AI coding agents
Points to the tension between approval fatigue and over-blocking as the core human-in-the-loop dilemma

stats.fact: Players missed roughly 1 in 3 threats — mean accuracy 66.3% across 40,000+ sessions and 409,000 approve/deny decisions
32.9% of sessions ended with a net-negative score (approved threats + blocked safe commands outweighed correct calls)
35.2% of players caught every threat, but only 20.8% did so while blocking at most 1 in 5 safe commands
7% of players approved every single prompt
Obviously destructive commands (rm -rf /, chmod -R 777 /) were missed only 11.7% of the time
Persistent mutation attacks (crontab injection, git config hijack) missed 23.8% of the time
Exfiltration/code execution attacks (curl to unknown APIs, typosquatted packages) missed 33.4% of the time
Scope violations (cat ~/.aws/credentials, cat ~/.kube/config) missed 35.0% of the time — credentials exfiltration missed ~3x more often than destructive commands
npm run analyze was the single most-missed command, approved 64.7% of the time despite the history log showing an exfiltration payload
Three camouflaged npm-script attacks (analyze, setup, deploy) pooled at 52.5% miss rate vs 28.4% for other exfiltration attacks — familiarity roughly doubles attack success
Over-blocking: npm config set registry blocked 59% of the time, rm -rf dist/ 45%, kill $(lsof -t -i:3000) 43% — all benign commands
cat ~/.zshrc was the most contested command, approved 45.9% of the time (risk depends on whether secrets live in the shell profile)
Miss rates climb toward the end of sessions — evidence of permission fatigue under accumulated approvals
Anthropic's internal study of 1,053 testers found the 'ask the user for everything' approach has an 86.4% miss rate; Auto mode (classifier-based) has ~11% miss rate
The game had ~34% threat density, far above real-world prevalence, and players knew they were being tested — so 66.3% accuracy is an optimistic ceiling, not a realistic floor

angles: Human-in-the-loop approval is measurably unreliable as a sole security safeguard — the 1-in-3 miss rate is a design-pattern failure, not a human failure
Permission fatigue is a real, measured effect: every added approval prompt taxes the vigilance available for the next one, and miss rates rise over a session
Familiar command names are the attack surface — npm run X always looks safe, and camouflaged scripts roughly double attack success (52.5% vs 28.4%)
The flip side of the dilemma: over-blocking benign commands (up to 59%) makes real agent workflows unusable and pushes developers toward full bypasses
Defense in depth is the answer: sandboxing + scoped/least-privilege credentials + surgical gating layered on top of human review, not instead of it
Read the script, not the command name — the npm run blind spot is the clearest single number in the dataset
Real-world parallels: Claude Memory Heist (exfiltration with no prompt at all) and Codex $HOME deletion (full-access mode bypassing sandboxing) show the same failure modes with real consequences
Anthropic's shift to Auto mode as default validates the data: classifier-based gating (11% miss) beats human review (86.4% miss) for routine commands
